en: Having prostrated before my own self, the Supreme Lord who is supreme bliss,
I shall speak the *Advaitaśataka*.
A Compendium of All the Vedāntas. ||1||
Mahādeva, whose nature is pure consciousness,
entering a body by his own will,
is declared in the Śruti to be the "jīvātman" (the individual soul).
The body is designated as "māyā. ||2||
Therefore, the body, which consists of the visible, is called the "seer" (dṛk-rūpa) for the sake of the embodied self;
thus, the seer [appears] in the form of the visible.
The circle of the elements is thus established. ||3||
Without the body, the individual soul (jīvātman) is not capable of doing anything; likewise, without the soul, the body [is incapable].
He is not capable of knowing or seeing it. ||4||
Therefore, the conscious self, having attained a relationship of identity with the body,
determines "I am the body."
He constantly performs actions. ||5||
The body of discerning human beings is said to be fourfold:
the gross, the subtle, and the causal.
And it is called by the names "the universal" (sāmānya). ||6||
Devoid of an ordinary body for those undiscriminating beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
The body is said to be threefold. ||7||
In the waking state, that which exists as the gross body is proclaimed to be the subtle body;
and in dream and deep sleep, it is likewise the body.
This is proclaimed as the *kāraṇākyam*. ||8||
All this visible form is designated as the "body" (deha); the supreme light pervading therein is celebrated as the "embodiment" (deha). ||9||
This is the common state of the body for discerning human beings; indeed,
it is called the fourth state (turya).
Extremely rare in all the worlds. ||10||
When a person’s abiding in this universal body arises, then he becomes a lord of yogis through the Vedas.
He is celebrated as the Supreme Self. ||11||
When the existence of humans occurs within gross and other bodies,
it is then called the "individual soul" (jīvātman).
Because it is grasped as a contraction by the wise. ||12||
For this living soul, wandering perpetually through the essence-less cycle of existence,
goes from world to another world.
He shall destroy the vessel of the womb. ||13||
Having departed from the inner sanctum, he entered the world of humans once more, [saying]: "This is my son, this is my wife."
This wealth is ours. ||14||
This is my lineage, this is my friend, this is my home; this is my mother, this is my father.
These people are my enemies. ||15||
Having thus resolved, the individual soul (jīvātman) indeed directs itself toward these very things— attachment and aversion— day after day.
It is solely due to one's own ignorance. ||16||
Of the one-formed God, the inner self of all,
whose body is pervading like space.
Of that which is of the nature of consciousness, at all times. ||17||
In some cases, because of the inclusion of illusion (māyā) and so forth, which have the nature of the visible,
[there is the inclusion] of everything that has the nature of the substratum.
Just as the sky is dependent upon the clouds. ||18||
The individual soul (jīva) creates a division within that which is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), by means of the conceptualization of Brahmā, Rudra, and others.
It is solely due to one's own ignorance. ||19||
For the contraction of the all-pervading Lord is indeed suffering;
it is that very [contraction] which the individual soul (jīva) undergoes.
It is solely due to one's own ignorance. ||20||
Now, for those devoid of truth,
who act out of desire, who follow their whims,
and who are averse to their own duty—
He always forms associations. ||21||
Furthermore, having remained both subject and non-subject together with them like a dog or a donkey,
one is liberated from all phenomena.
The body indeed serves those very [objects]. ||22||
In conversation with the fawn-eyed women, in their glances, touches, and the like,
and in their laughter, emotions, and graceful charms.
The mind sinks completely [into it]. ||23||
From the grasping of sense objects, hatred arises in a living being toward mother, father, and son.
And one should show respect toward elders in the presence of other people. ||24||
A living being who has not attained his object suffers through anxiety, which is joined with grief, delusion, fear, affliction, anger, and greed. (25)
Upon obtaining it, there is supreme joy accompanied by a hundredfold good fortune;
having meditated upon a hundred intentions, [one should proceed].
It becomes attached to sense objects. ||26||
When an object has not been obtained, or even when it has been obtained,
a living being finds no benefit;
such is the case within the pits of sensory objects.
The young man polishes it thoroughly. ||27||
Having cultivated friendship with them, the individual soul constantly thinks, "This is mine," regarding their suffering day after day.
[This occurs] due to the merit performed in previous births. ||28||
Day after day, experience the fruition of your prārabdha karma through human effort and exertion.
He constantly performs actions. ||29||
For men existing in saṃsāra, by that very cause,
there arise actions that are both auspicious and inauspicious.
The doctrine of Sanmati is twofold. ||30||
If human actions— both auspicious and inauspicious— did not exist, [then] the injunctions of the Vedas...
It certainly becomes purposeless. ||31||
"One should not harm any living beings,
nor should one do harm to the virtuous"—
such are the words [of the scriptures].
Indeed, they are devoid of meaning when subjected to investigation. ||32||
Otherwise, for whom do injunctive statements function? If it is said that they function with respect to the individual soul (jīva), [then...]
He too is subject to the power of karma. ||33||
The living being follows its karma and indeed conforms to its actions;
therefore, when karma is exhausted, [the being is liberated].
For him, death will certainly occur. ||34||
For those fools who, out of delusion, do not accept the twofold nature of karma,
death itself is indeed liberation.
It is certainly like that of a materialist. ||35||
Having thus assumed a gross body and experienced both the auspicious and inauspicious through human effort by means of the subtle body, [one departs].
He begins to eat once again. ||36||
The departure of the subtle body from the gross body is known as death;
at the time of death for living beings, this is proclaimed to be the subtle body. (37)
Through the exhaustion of prārabdha karma by means of experience, the conscious self involuntarily effects the withdrawal from the gross body into the subtle body. ||38||
Just as in a dream the subtle body exists apart from the gross body, so it is for persons at the time of death.
The persistence of the subtle body shall occur. ||39||
Whatever action the conscious being performs in a dream by means of the subtle body,
the individual soul performs it by means of the gross body.
At that time, it performs that very same [action]. ||40||
Having thus abandoned the gross body and assumed a subtle form,
[one goes] either to heaven or even to hell.
The individual soul departs. ||41||
Due to an abundance of merit,
the individual soul causes the heavenly world to blossom in due order for the sake of enjoyment.
In its own nature, by its own cognition. ||42||
Pure consciousness alone is one,
yet it appears as threefold in a dream,
through the forms of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped.
so shall it be in the heavenly world. ||43||
Whatever may be the material cause of the manifold world of dreams, that itself is the cause of heaven and likewise of hell.
Grasping itself would come into being. ||44||
The individual soul, having gone to heaven or indeed to hell with the subtle body (liṅgadeha),
subsequently experiences the auspicious and inauspicious results that consist of the mind.
Having entered the body, which is the cause and is entirely composed of mind,
one attains great happiness, casting off all exhaustion.
Having abandoned the causal body,
which is marvelous and consists of the knowledge of one's own self,
[one abides] in the perfectly purified white fortnight.
He became awakened within the womb-vessel. ||47||
Then, having understood from within the womb that the menstrual flow was pure and white,
she took it as her limiting adjunct (upādhi).
It is said that he desires only the body itself. ||48||
A man who, having first fallen into a state of unconsciousness, causes [the fetus] to remain within the womb brings much misfortune.
[It arises] from the wholesome and unwholesome [karma] of previous lives. ||49||
Having meditated again and again upon the body itself as being beginningless by way of its continuous flow, through the power of time,
The body itself is born. ||50||
When, having taken on the state of being a limiting adjunct (upādhi), it remains as the white menstrual flow (śuklārtava),
it exists without a body.
How, then, can there be meditative absorption at that time? ||51||
Of the Lord, whose sole nature is pure consciousness and whose form is bliss,
there is no limitation within His own essential nature.
Māyā may be that which belongs to the Supreme Lord. ||52||
"For one devoid of knowledge, thinking 'I am indeed the very consciousness-nature of the God who is consciousness-nature'— "
Awakening is said to be illusion. ||53||
When investigated in this way, divine illusion (māyā) is postulated;
by it, [the soul] undergoes contraction.
Bondage is said here to be beginningless. ||54||
Illusion, which has neither beginning nor end, abides in the investigation of illusion;
this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, [is that illusion].
Because it is its effect, it must be so. ||55||
For this very reason, the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) toward the Lord, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
becomes firmly established in each of the seven wombs.
For that reason, among men existing in the worlds,
the ego-sense persists even without a body.
It proceeds by the power of latent impressions. ||57||
Just as a tree, complete with branches and the like, resides within a seed,
so too does the body reside within me.
Endowed with hands, feet, and so forth. ||58||
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), joined with ignorance and the rest, brings about its residence in the womb solely through the power of egoism (ahaṅkāra).
The body itself is born. ||59||
Having emerged from the womb once more, this person, with a fully formed body, [arises] due to the auspicious and inauspicious karma of previous births.
He fell into a state of great astonishment and fainted. ||60||
Thus, O embodied one, as you wander while maintaining your presence within the three bodies,
you are called the "individual self" (jīvātman) by the wise.
by those who have reached the further shore of all the Vedāntas. ||61||
Thus, for a person wandering in saṃsāra, [liberation] arises solely from the sight of the Teacher, based on the merit and demerit earned by oneself.
Dispassion arises in the heart. ||62||
Thus, in the heart of the man endowed with dispassion, the pure Self manifested continuously.
Such is this reflection. ||63||
What joy indeed could there be for men through wealth, which is sown with suffering and is as difficult to obtain as one's own death?
Always in the form of evil. ||64||
What use have I for a home, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth— even that of Kubera—
and what purpose do friends and kinsmen serve?
Everything is non-existent due to the power of time. //65//
What is the use of a woman who is the embodiment of evil, or what is the use of sons who are causes of misery,
for one who is being seized by death?
What purpose is served by them moment after moment? ||66||
In birth after birth, many sons and wives have passed away for those experiencing the fruits of their past karma.
What fruit is there for men in this world by means of those [worldly things]? ||67||
For a man who speaks the truth and is free from attachment to worldly existents, [the inquiry arises]:
"Who am I? And how is this?"
The thought should be well-expert and confident. ||68||
She [directed] her thought toward a Brahmin guide,
one endowed with the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas,
and possessed of the knowledge of Brahman among men.
It accomplishes the boon in an instant. ||69||
This individual soul, purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta), having beheld the form of the Guru, becomes subject to another's will.
And he bowed down again and again. ||70||
Having bowed to the high-souled Lord, the compassionate Teacher,
in order to fully realize one's own true nature...
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed him.
O Teacher, I desire to know the true nature of supreme bliss for those who wish to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
You are the helmsman for embodied beings. ||72||
Thus questioned by his dispassionate disciple, the knower of the supreme truth,
meditating upon his own true nature, replied:
The guide spoke to him.
That depending upon which all people continuously function—
one should know that to be the true nature (svarūpa).
By the instruments, such as the eyes and so forth. ||74||
That which the gross body depends upon during the waking state,
the subtle body likewise depends upon during the dream state.
The wise know him to be their own true nature. ||75||
But in deep sleep, that unmanifest body consisting of one's own ignorance shines forth, depending upon which [the state exists] as the causal form.
Ascertain its true nature. ||76||
That which appears in false forms through the distinctions of waking and so forth, [is known] by its nature as the witness of those states.
He alone is the Supreme Lord. ||77||
You alone are Śiva, Viṣṇu, Agni, Indra, and the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are Sūrya and Soma; you are the Teacher (Śāstṛ) and Vināyaka. ||78||
She is proclaimed by the wise under various names such as Vāṇī, Śrī, Girijā, Durgā, Devī, and so forth; this is due to differences in their understanding, and not otherwise. (79)
When that embodied being, relying upon a single form, performs both conceptualization and discursive thought, [he becomes bound].
then it is called "mind" (manas). ||80||
When the inner self has abandoned doubt and its form has been discerned, [then...]
then it is called "intellect" (buddhi). ||81||
When, through self-reflection,
he clearly cognizes the form as "this is thus."
Then he would possess egoism. ||82||
Just as "hand" and "arm" are indeed synonyms for the arm, so too are "mind," "intellect," "ego," and "consciousness" synonyms for the self. (83)
Just as from the difference in the wick of a lamp,
or from the specific manner of cooking sugarcane,
there arises a distinction consisting of name and form.
That [is] thus for the living being, not otherwise. ||84||
Just as ghee is pervaded by milk, so is the Supreme Person present within the visible world;
yet, due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there appears to be a distinction.
Therefore, for a single [entity], it cannot be otherwise. ||85||
Mahādeva is of one form,
abiding within all beings;
the great ether is of one form.
Just as it exists in jars and other such objects. ||86||
And because there is no dispute regarding bodies that exist individually,
yet are all endowed with hands, feet, and so forth.
There is no difference when analyzed. ||87||
This entire universe, both moving and non-moving, is known to consist of the five elements;
[so too are] the bodies composed of the five elements.
There is no differentiation when things remain in that state. ||87||
Just as there is no difference between jars and other objects because they consist of clay,
so too [there is no difference] because [all things] consist of the five elements.
And likewise for bodies as well. ||89||
When one reflects in this way, my dear,
there is never any distinction between the bodies and the five elements.
Of those that are inert and quickly perishable. ||90||
In this world, one who possesses the conviction, "I am this [soul] consisting of nine spaces (pradeśas), measured by hands, feet, and so forth," [is a person of worldly certainty].
It is designated as the "living being" (jīva). ||91||
"I am complete everywhere, and this body is likewise so"—
thus is one who possesses internal certainty.
He is called the Supreme Self. ||92||
This being the case, there would be no distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
rather, there would be only their non-difference.
Because there is no difference in the nature of consciousness. ||13||
If it is argued that the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is the witness of the body, that is not tenable;
for [during] deep sleep, all bodies...
Precisely because of its insentience, and not otherwise. ||14||
The vital breath (prāṇa) performs its own function; it is not the maker of the body, as seen from the cessation of the body [at death].
Understand it in this way. ||95||
Whatever is thought by the king, that his dependents perform;
therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) cannot be the agent.
Because it is observed thus in the world. ||96||
Completely abandoning the latent impressions born of the three bodies,
and having assumed the supreme body.
May the higher existence be fulfilled. //97//
Having fully assumed this form, both auspicious and inauspicious,
one performs the obligatory and occasional rites.
One who acts thus constantly is not defiled. ||98||
Actions performed by living beings in the world through speech, mind, and body—how can the agent [be held responsible] for any one of these [results] based on mere satisfaction? (99)
Having experienced Śiva— who is omnipresent, tranquil, and designated as one's own true nature—
one abandons the body.
Become one who consists of mere cognition.
